items.prose: A pair $(X, Y)$ has density $f(x, y) = 3x$ on the triangle $0 \le y \le x \le 1$, and 0 elsewhere. Its volume is 1.
items.question: What is $P(X \le 0.5)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the marginal $f_X$ first, integrating $y$ over its slice $0$ to $x$.

byKey.rect: 0.375 integrates $y$ from 0 to 1. At the line through $x$ the triangle only has $y$ up to $x$.
byKey.half: 0.5 would hold if $X$ were uniform. Its marginal $3x^2$ is far lower near 0.

explain.text: The marginal is $3x^2$, so the cumulative chance is $x^3$, and $0.5^3 = 0.125$. The slice at $x$ is as long as the triangle is tall there.

items.title: A marginal from a triangle

items.prose: $X$ is uniform on $[0, 1]$ and $Y = X^2$, so $x = \sqrt y$ and $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right| = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}$.
items.question: What is the density $f_Y(0.16)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $f_X(\sqrt y) = 1$ by $\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}$.

byKey.nofac: 1 is $f_X$ alone. The factor $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$ is missing.
byKey.inv: 0.8 is $2\sqrt y$, the factor upside down. You need $\left|\tfrac{dx}{dy}\right|$, not $\left|\tfrac{dy}{dx}\right|$.

explain.text: Squaring squeezes the small values of $X$ together, so $Y$ is dense near 0: $f_Y(y) = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt y}$, which is 1.25 at $y = 0.16$.

items.title: A square of a uniform

items.prose: Two independent fill times are uniform on $[0, 1]$. The density of the sum is $t$ on $[0, 1]$ and $2 - t$ on $[1, 2]$.
items.question: What is $P(U_1 + U_2 > 1.2)$?

feedback.correct: The tail is a triangle of base and height 0.8: $\tfrac12 \times 0.8 \times 0.8 = 0.32$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The tail beyond 1.2 is a small triangle under $2 - t$.

byKey.unif: 0.4 treats the sum as uniform on $[0, 2]$: $\tfrac{0.8}{2}$. The triangle puts less mass at the ends.
byKey.sq: 0.64 is $0.8^2$: the area of a square. A triangle has half of that.

explain.text: $\int_{1.2}^{2}(2 - t)\,dt = \tfrac{0.8^2}{2} = 0.32$. The density falls to 0 at 2, so the tail is triangular.

items.title: Two fills, late

items.prose: Five independent waits are exponential with rate 0.5 a year. The CDF of one is $1 - e^{-0.5t}$.
items.question: What is the chance that all five waits are at most 3 years, $P(\max \le 3)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All five must be at most 3: raise the single chance to the fifth power.

byKey.single: 0.7769 is the chance for one wait. All five must finish.
byKey.comp: 0.717 is $1 - 0.283$, the chance that at least one wait exceeds 3 years.

items.title: All five finished

items.prose: Ten skill-free strategies have independent $t$-ratios, each roughly $N(0, 1)$. One of them is reported, the largest.
items.question: What is the chance that the largest is at least 2?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that all ten stay below 2, then subtract from 1.

byKey.single: 0.0228 is the chance for one strategy. Ten tries make it much larger.
byKey.times: 0.2275 is $10 \times 0.0228$. It overcounts the cases where two or more clear 2.

explain.text: $\Phi(2)^{10} = 0.7944$ is the chance that none reaches 2, so the best does with chance 0.2056. One in five fund pitches this good is luck.

items.title: The best of ten

items.prose: Orders arrive at 3 a minute. The wait for the second order has density $9te^{-3t}$ and tail $P(T > t) = e^{-3t}(1 + 3t)$.
items.question: What is the chance the second order takes more than a minute?

byKey.first: 0.0498 is $e^{-3}$, the chance the first order takes over a minute. The second takes longer.

explain.text: $e^{-3}\times 4 = 0.1991$. Equivalently, fewer than 2 orders arrive in a minute: Poisson(3) gives $e^{-3}(1 + 3)$.

items.title: The second arrival

items.prose: A hit rate has a uniform prior, Beta(1, 1). The strategy wins 7 of 10 trades.
items.question: Which is the posterior?

options.why: You used the counts alone and dropped the prior. The prior's 1 and 1 are added in.
You swapped wins and losses. Wins add to the first parameter.
You added all 10 trades to $a$. Only the 7 wins go to $a$, and the 3 losses go to $b$.

feedback.correct: Wins add to $a$: $1 + 7 = 8$. Losses add to $b$: $1 + 3 = 4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the wins to $a$ and the losses to $b$.

explain.text: The likelihood $p^7(1 - p)^3$ times the flat prior is $p^{8-1}(1 - p)^{4-1}$, a Beta(8, 4), with mean $\tfrac{8}{12} = 0.667$.

items.title: A Beta posterior

items.prose: An exponential variable has MGF $M(t) = \dfrac{2}{2 - t}$ for $t < 2$.
items.question: What is $E[X] = M'(0)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $2(2 - t)^{-1}$ and set $t = 0$.

byKey.rate: 2 is the rate $\lambda$. The mean is $\tfrac1\lambda$.
byKey.value: 1 is $M(0)$, which is always 1. The mean is the slope $M'(0)$.

explain.text: $M'(t) = 2(2 - t)^{-2}$, so $M'(0) = \tfrac24 = \tfrac12$, the mean of an exponential with rate 2.

items.title: Reading a mean from an MGF

items.prose: Counts $N_1 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(2)$ and $N_2 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(3)$ are independent, with MGFs $e^{2(e^t - 1)}$ and $e^{3(e^t - 1)}$.
items.question: What is the distribution of $N_1 + N_2$?

options.why: The MGFs multiply, but their exponents add: $2 + 3 = 5$, not $2 \times 3$.
You averaged the means. A sum of counts adds them.
The product $e^{5(e^t - 1)}$ is exactly the Poisson(5) MGF, and an MGF identifies the distribution.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two MGFs and read off the form.

explain.text: The product is the MGF of a Poisson with mean 5, and an MGF identifies a distribution. Independent Poisson counts add their means.

items.title: Two Poisson streams
